title: Ibn Khaldun: Thinking About History
summary: The life of Ibn Khaldun, the North African scholar who taught that historians must check reports for evidence and causes, and who explained how groups rise and fall.
poll: It is important to check a story before you believe it.

versions.title: A Man Who Thought About the Past
versions.text:
Long ago, a boy was born in Tunis. The year was 1332. His name was Ibn Khaldun.

He loved to read. He loved to learn. But when he was a teen, a bad sickness came. It was the plague. His mom and dad both died.

He grew up. Then he worked for kings. He moved from land to land. Some kings liked him. Some did not!

Then he went to a fort. It was quiet there. He stayed for four years. He wrote a big book. It was a book of history.

He had a new idea. We must check old tales, he said. Could this tale be true? What made it happen? Do not just copy what you hear.

He also said this. Groups get strong when they stick close. When they stop helping each other, they get weak.

Late in his life, he lived in Cairo. He was a judge there. He died in 1406.

People still read his book. They read it all over the world. They say he helped start a new way to look at how we live.

versions.title: Ibn Khaldun: Thinking About History
versions.text:
In 1332, a boy named Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis, a city in North Africa. His family had moved there from al-Andalus, the Muslim lands in what is now Spain. He grew up surrounded by books and teachers.

When he was a teenager, a terrible disease called the plague swept across many countries. Both of his parents died. Still, he kept studying, and he became known as a brilliant young scholar.

As an adult, Ibn Khaldun worked for rulers in many lands across North Africa and Spain. His life was full of change. Some rulers trusted him, while others threw him in prison!

Later, he moved to a quiet fort far from the cities. There, in about four years, he wrote a long work called the Introduction. It was the opening part of a huge history of the world.

In the Introduction, he explained how a good historian should work. He said we must check old reports before we believe them. Is there evidence? Could the event really have happened? What caused it?

He also wrote about solidarity, the feeling that holds a group together. A group with strong solidarity can rise to power. Over time, though, rulers grow comfortable, the feeling fades, and the group grows weak.

In his last years, he lived in Cairo, Egypt, where he worked as a judge. He died there in 1406.

Today, many people call him one of the first thinkers to study how societies work.

versions.title: Ibn Khaldun: The Scholar Who Questioned History
versions.text:
In 1332, Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis, in North Africa, into a family that had migrated from al-Andalus, the Muslim lands in what is now Spain. Surrounded by books and respected teachers, he showed remarkable talent as a young scholar.

When he was a teenager, the plague swept across North Africa and much of the world, and both of his parents died. Nevertheless, he continued his education and soon entered the service of powerful rulers.

For more than twenty years, Ibn Khaldun held positions in royal courts across North Africa and Spain. His career was unpredictable, because some rulers trusted him with important responsibilities, while others imprisoned him when politics shifted.

Eventually, he withdrew to a remote fortress, where in about four years he wrote the Muqaddimah, an Arabic word meaning "Introduction." Completed in 1377, it was the opening section of an enormous history of the world, yet it became more famous than the history itself.

In the Muqaddimah, Ibn Khaldun argued that a historian must not simply copy earlier reports. Instead, he should examine the evidence, ask whether an event was actually possible, and search for its causes.

He also described solidarity, which he called asabiyyah, the loyalty that binds a group together. A group with strong solidarity can found a new dynasty, but after about three generations, its rulers grow comfortable, the bond weakens, and the dynasty declines.

He even studied how people earn a living, noting that work creates wealth and that very heavy taxes make people stop working and trading.

He also believed that the land and the weather where people live shape the way they work, eat, and build their towns.

In 1401, while visiting Damascus, he met Timur, a powerful conqueror whose army had surrounded the city, and the two men discussed history for many days.

He spent his final years in Cairo, serving as a judge until his death in 1406. Today, many scholars regard him as a pioneer of sociology, the study of how societies function and change.

versions.title: Ibn Khaldun: The Scholar Who Questioned History
versions.text:
In 1332, Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis, in North Africa, into a distinguished family that had migrated from al-Andalus, the Muslim lands in what is now Spain. Surrounded by books and respected teachers, he demonstrated remarkable intellectual talent as a young scholar, mastering language, law, and philosophy.

When he was a teenager, the plague swept across North Africa and much of the world, and both of his parents perished, leaving him to make his own way in a frightening world. Nevertheless, he persisted with his education and soon entered the service of powerful rulers, beginning a turbulent career that would take him across an entire region.

For more than twenty years, Ibn Khaldun held positions in royal courts across North Africa and Spain. His career was remarkably unpredictable, because some rulers entrusted him with significant responsibilities, while others imprisoned him whenever political loyalties shifted.

Eventually, he withdrew to a remote fortress, where in approximately four years he composed the Muqaddimah, an Arabic word meaning "Introduction." Completed in 1377, it was the opening section of an enormous history of the world, yet it ultimately became considerably more celebrated than the history itself.

In the Muqaddimah, Ibn Khaldun argued that a historian must not simply repeat earlier reports, however famous their authors might be. Instead, a responsible historian should scrutinize the evidence, consider whether an event was actually possible, and investigate its underlying causes.

He also analyzed solidarity, which he called asabiyyah, the loyalty that binds a community together. A group with strong solidarity can establish a new dynasty, but after approximately three generations, its rulers become accustomed to luxury, the bond deteriorates, and the dynasty inevitably declines.

He even examined economics, observing that human labor generates wealth and that excessively heavy taxes discourage people from working and trading, which eventually reduces the government's own income. He also believed that the land and the weather where people live shape the way they work, eat, and build their towns.

In 1401, while visiting Damascus, he encountered Timur, a formidable conqueror whose army had surrounded the city, and the two men discussed history and geography for many days, after which he wrote a long and careful report about the meeting.

He spent his final years in Cairo, serving as a judge until his death in 1406. Today, many scholars regard him as a pioneer of sociology, the systematic study of how societies function and transform over time.

LOW.prompt: Ibn Khaldun said we should check a story before we believe it. Write about a time when you heard a story and wanted to check if it was true. What questions did you ask?
checklist: I told about a real or made-up story.
I wrote at least two questions to check it.
I used the word check correctly.
LOW.modelAnswer: Once my friend told me that a famous athlete had quit the team, but I was not sure it was true. I asked, is there real evidence for this, and who first heard the story, before I decided to check it myself and found out it was not true.

MID.prompt: Explain Ibn Khaldun's idea about solidarity. Then give an example of a team or group today where working together makes it stronger.
checklist: I explained solidarity in my own words.
I gave a clear example from today.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Solidarity, in my own words, is the strong sense of loyalty and teamwork that holds a group together and helps it succeed. Ibn Khaldun explained that a group with strong solidarity can rise to power, but over several generations the feeling can fade and the group grows weak. A sports team today shows this idea well, because when every player feels loyal to the team and works together, the whole team becomes much stronger than any one player alone.

HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree with Ibn Khaldun that solidarity helps a group rise while comfort can make it fall. The article explains that a group with strong solidarity, or shared loyalty, can rise to power, but as rulers in a dynasty grow comfortable over several generations, that feeling of solidarity fades and the group grows weak. I see the same pattern in a successful company today, where a small team that starts out working closely together can lose its drive once it becomes large and comfortable, echoing the pattern Ibn Khaldun first described centuries ago.
